desc:
You are given a string s of lowercase letters and an integer k. In one step you choose k consecutive positions that all hold the same letter and delete them; the left and right parts then join together. Repeat for as long as it is possible.

Return the final string. The final string is the same whichever valid deletion you choose first. It may be empty.

Example: with s = 'deeedbbcccbdaa' and k = 3, delete eee to get 'ddbbcccbdaa', delete ccc to get 'ddbbbdaa', delete bbb to get 'dddaa', delete ddd to get 'aa'.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: After a deletion, new runs of equal letters can appear, so a single left-to-right scan that only looks at the original runs is not enough.
What you need to know about the letters kept so far is: what is the last letter, and how many copies of it are in a row at the end?
Keep a stack of pairs (letter, run length). A new equal letter increases the top count; when the count reaches k pop the pair. A different letter pushes (letter, 1).
editorial: Store the kept characters as runs: a stack of [letter, count]. For each incoming letter, if the top run has the same letter, increase its count and pop the whole run if the count is now k. Otherwise push a new run [letter, 1].

Popping a run makes the run below it the new top, so letters on both sides of a deleted block can merge into one run, exactly as in the process described. The counts on the stack are always less than k. At the end expand each run into letter * count and join. The scan is O(n) time and O(n) space.
